item.title: How We Tested RAG: Found the Document, But Still Made a Mistake
item.description:

item.title: Former Engineers Never Exist: OCR and Translation of 65 Pages of Control System Calculations for Surgut-2 Power Station Turbogenerators
item.description:
Dear IT specialists, allow me to introduce myself: I am Savelyeva Victorina Yuryevna. I am reminding you of myself. 40 years ago, I completed a project commissioned by the Surgut-2 Power Station's operations department: "Study of the Dynamics of 800 MW Turbogenerators using the Logarithmic Amplitude-Frequency Characteristics Method." The published material may still be stored in the power station's archives. I only have a draft from 40 years ago. In August of this year, I experienced unexpected success by publishing its digitized copy on Habr. Despite my age (I turned 88 today) and the fact that I have been far from engineering for many years (I am now an artist), it is strange and unexpected, even for myself, that I realized: there are no former engineers. After carefully reviewing my first sensational draft, I was horrified to discover many inconsistencies and even errors. Most importantly, the final Logarithmic Amplitude-Frequency Characteristics of the open-loop voltage control system, which can be used to judge the qualities of the turbogenerator's closed-loop control system, is missing. It is possible that the final copy sent to the Surgut-2 Power Station forty years ago was modified. Life in Ottawa dictated its own terms: performing a huge amount of OCR recognition and coding in Russian did not make practical sense for me. I immediately translated the work into technical English. For modern specialists and readers of Habr, this language has long been the working language, and translating the control system calculations according to international IEEE standards makes this publication ready for integration into the global engineering community.

item.title: How We Built an AI Negotiator That Doesn't Yield: From Prompt to Deployment
item.description:
Spoiler: our experiment is repeatable! Hello, Habr! My name is Ksenia Kalabushkina, I am a training manager at the Corporate University of KORUS Consulting Group. At KORUS, we pay a lot of attention to developing our employees' negotiation skills: we regularly hold company-wide negotiation tournaments, organize training sessions and webinars, and invite external experts. This year, my team and I started thinking about how we could use AI for such a task. We experimented a lot and as a result created an AI negotiator – a service that allows you to play out a negotiation duel, get feedback, and recommendations for future skill development. I am not a programmer and have never written a line of code in my life. In this article, I will explain in detail how to create such a service without development skills and how to deploy it so that it becomes accessible to colleagues, and I will also share my recommendations and life hacks in vibe coding. The material will be useful to everyone who values the development of negotiation skills and is interested in creating their own AI applications, even if you don't know how to code. Read more

item.title: Parimatch Owner Invested in a Non-Existent AI Startup Due to Deepfake Deception
item.description:
Sergey Portnov, the owner of the betting company Parimatch, was tricked into investing in a non-existent AI startup using a deepfake of an acquaintance. While Portnov did not disclose the amount, he stated it was "very expensive." He warned that scams are no longer limited to "bank employees" but can now involve friends or relatives, with familiar voices and personal details, even through video calls, as deepfakes have become frighteningly high-quality. Read more

item.title: Enthusiast Launches DeepSeek-V4-Flash on a PC Without a Graphics Card
item.description:
The llama-modchip project, released under Apache 2.0, offers patches for ggml/llama.cpp kernels, quantization tools, and scripts to run sparse MoE models directly on the CPU. The author claims DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284 billion parameters, 13 billion active) runs on a machine with 64GB of RAM, without a graphics card or swap. This article explores what was achieved.

item.title: It's Not AI That Devalued Seniority. Your Interviews Did.
item.description:
It's commonly believed that LLMs devalue experience: a junior with a model produces results similar to an expert's, making expertise seem unnecessary. Data reveals a more complex picture. While models do narrow the gap on tasks they excel at, they don't provide juniors with the crucial ability to verify answers. It's not the model, but the hiring process that equates juniors with LLMs and experienced specialists, by focusing only on areas where they are similar. Let's explore how this happens and what hiring adaptations can be justified by research.

item.title: We created an AI bot for daily business metric analysis
item.description:
Hi! We are BI developers: Aigul Akhmetova from the Avito Advertising analytics team and Valeriya Smirnova from Goods. Together we create analytical reports that help teams understand business metrics faster. We also created a bot that took some of the routine off the analysts' shoulders. The Core BI team is responsible for the main financial dashboard. Every morning starts roughly the same: 1. Open the main financial report. 2. Check if the data has been updated. 3. Look at revenue dynamics and go through the breakdowns. 4. If the figure has changed significantly, figure out where exactly and why. To do this, we involve metric analysts from different teams. 5. Briefly explain the result to colleagues, and if something is wrong with the data, warn them when it will be ready. Nothing supernatural, but these actions take at least half an hour every day. Not because each time a complex investigation or deep dive into details is required. It's just that between looking at a graph and answering the question "What happened?" there are several mandatory checks – they cannot be skipped. We decided to automate this part of the work and created Big10 Pulse – a bot in the corporate messenger Mattermost. It monitors key business metrics daily. As soon as fresh data is ready, it sends a PDF report and an analytical note with a factor analysis of changes and found deviations. This way, the analyst doesn't have to repeat the same actions every day, and the user doesn't have to constantly check if the data has been updated. It sounds like an ideal task for a large language model – as we like it: collect context from different sources and threads, and then explain the found anomaly. But we quickly realized that the main thing here is not what work can be entrusted to the model, but what cannot.

item.title: Meta* made its smallest model a workhorse for agents
item.description:
After the release of giant and expensive neural networks, one wants to find something that fits the concepts of economy and specialization. And on November 9, Meta*'s Superintelligence Labs released Muse Ember, the smallest and cheapest model in its lineup. It is designed specifically for mass and routine work: calling tools, routing, and parsing documents in AI pipelines. The new combination is described as follows: Muse Wonder plans the work, and Ember executes it. Let's break down what the release is based on. Read more

item.title: Mascot for Claude Code: How to know when the assistant is waiting for a response and not miss Windows notifications
item.description:
I often give Claude Code a long task and switch to another window. After ten to fifteen minutes, I return and see that it has long been stuck on the question "can I execute this command?" and has been waiting all this time. The Windows system notification, of course, was shown, but for five seconds in the corner while I was looking elsewhere. I didn't want to remind myself with a timer; I needed something impossible to miss. As a result, I created a mascot: a small orange figure that peeks out from the bottom right corner of the screen, and if ignored, emerges completely, turns red, and starts stomping on the taskbar. Below, I'll explain how it works. The main challenges turned out not to be in the animation, but in two things: how to know at all that Claude is waiting, and how to draw a window that is visible above everything else but doesn't interfere with anything. Read more

item.title: How a website can get clicks from Google's AI Overviews if a neural network writes the page description
item.description:
Google is testing short page summaries directly in source cards within AI Overviews. According to Search Engine Roundtable, these summaries appear to the right and below the AI Overviews response, allowing users to read what the AI said about the page before deciding to click. Essentially, this is a new snippet (a short description of the page in search results) written by an AI model for the website owner. Therefore, it's now crucial to check the page's first screen and direct answers: if the summary doesn't clearly explain why someone should visit, they won't click. Read more
